title: Anzu, Standard Babylonian Tablet I: the theft of the Tablet of Destinies
source: British Museum and Yale Peabody Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.10, Anzu, SB I) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: The Epic of Anzu, Standard Babylonian Tablet I: 183 of 201 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (4 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
A hymn to Ninurta introduces the poem. Anzu, set to guard Enlil's bath, seizes the Tablet of Destinies and flies off; the gods look for a champion, and Adad, Gerra and Shara refuse.

The Epic of Anzu tells how the lion-headed bird Anzu stole the Tablet of Destinies from Enlil, and how the god Ninurta, after other gods refused, defeated Anzu and recovered it. The Standard Babylonian version has three tablets. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/10/SB/I) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so (K.7257). The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the text; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 183 of the 201 lines of the eBL edition (91%), from 4 tablets in the British Museum and Yale Peabody Museum: K.7257 (Nineveh), YBC.9842, K.3454 (Nineveh), K.22880 (Nineveh).

Lines not shown. 18 of the 201 lines of the eBL edition are not shown, because no photographed copy of the work used here carries them: b+110-b+124 (no manuscript preserves it); b+181-b+182 (its photographs do not show which lines these are: YBC.9842); c+190 (its photographs do not show which lines these are: YBC.9842). A line is shown only on a photographed tablet that carries it as text. Commentaries and other texts that quote a line (letters, rituals, god lists) are not used as witnesses, because they carry it with explanations or inside another text; tablets without a photograph in eBL are not used, because the line could not be shown on its tablet.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; ... broken signs of unknown number; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; / alternative readings; (line break) the line runs on to the next line of the tablet; (blank space) a space left by the scribe.

translation.text:
1Son of the king of the inhabited world, splendid one, beloved of [Ma]mi,
2The mighty one will I ever sing, divine firstborn of [En]lil,
3Ninurta, the splendid one, beloved of Mami,
4The mighty one will I ever praise, divine firstborn of Enlil.
5Born (in) Ekur, leader of the Anu[nna-gods], Eninnu’s hope,
6Who waters paddock, garden, town, street, and city,
7Wave of battles, dancer (in combat), sash of valor,
8Whose tireless onset raging fiends dread,
9Hear the praise of the mighty one’s strength!
10It is he who in his fierceness defeated and fettered the mount of stones,
11Conquering soaring Anzu with his weapon,
translation.scan_note: British Museum K.7257: obverse, the tablet's own lines 2' to 12'. eBL's corpus edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/10/SB/I) attributes SB I 1-11 to this manuscript at these column and line numbers. Photograph checked: one face of a fragment about 4 cm wide with about 15 lines, ink K.7257 on the right edge. Consistent with eBL's obverse 15. eBL classes K.7257 as a tablet that eBL classes as 'Varia' (not a library copy of the series), not a library copy of the whole work. It carries these lines as text (eBL's transliteration has no commentary or quotation markup), and it is used because no photographed library copy preserves these lines as well. On this tablet lines 1-11 are partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of these lines translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken.

12Slaying the bull man in the midst of the sea.
13Doughty, valorous, slaughterer with his weapon,
14Mighty one, impetuous, leader of battle and fray!
15Until then, no daises had been built among the Igigi-gods,
16It was the Igigi-gods who knelt in their supremacy.
17Tigris and [Euph]rates rivers had been fashioned,
18But the [springs] were not bearing [their?] waters to the land.
19The very seas […],
20Clouds were […] together at the horizon.
21Then were the [Igigi-gods] convened from all parts,

23Did his children bring [the news],
24“Hee[d? you well] the propitious word!

26“In her lap the Anu[nna-gods …]
27“She bore Anzu […]
28“[His] pinions a saw […]

translation.text:
b+58And assigned to all the [gods] their responsibilities.
b+59Destiny reversing so that Anzu would hold […],
b+60Enlil entrusted him with the entrance to the sanctuary he had finished.
b+61He being wont to bathe in pure waters in his presence,
b+62His eyes would look upon the trappings of supremacy,
b+63On his lordly crown, his divine apparel,
b+64On the tablet of destinies in his hands Anzu was wont to gaze.
b+65He was wont to gaze, indeed, at the father of the gods, divine Duranki,
b+66He resolved in his heart to make off with supremacy.
b+67Anzu was wont to gaze on the father of the gods, divine Duranki,
b+68He resolved in his heart to make off with supremacy!
b+69“Let me be the one to take the gods’ tablet of destinies,
b+70“Then I will appropriate for myself the responsibilities of all the gods,
b+71“I will have the throne for myself, I will take power over divine authority,
b+72“I will give orders to each and every Igigi-god.”
b+73His heart plotted the assault,
b+74At the entrance to the sanctuary, where he was wont to gaze, he was waiting for morn.
b+75When Enlil was bathing in the pure waters,
b+76Undressed, his crown set on the throne,
b+77He took hold of the tablet of destinies,
b+78He took supremacy for himself, [divine authority] was overthrown.
b+79Anzu soared off and [made his way] to his mountain,
b+80Awful silence befell, deathly sti[llness] reigned.
b+81Their father and counsellor Enlil was speechless,
b+82The sanctuary shed its divine splendor.
b+83The gods of the land converged, one after another, for a plan.

translation.text:
b+84Anu made ready to speak,
b+85Saying to the gods his children,
b+86“O gods, which one of you would slay Anzu?
b+87“Let him make his the greatest name in the entire inhabited world.”
b+88They summoned the Irrigator, Anu’s son,
b+89Plan in mind, he said to him,
b+90They summoned Adad, the irrigator, Anu’s son,
b+91Plan in mind, he said to him,
b+92“O mighty Adad, ferocious Adad, let your battle not turn back,
b+93“Blitz Anzu with your weapon.
b+94“Let your [name] be greatest among all the great gods,
b+95“You shall have no equal [among] the gods your brethren.
b+96“Let there be daises to you, let them be built,
